pages.name: Under water, the states, and the phone

artboards.title: Proposed — the line goes under, and naming a day
Proposed — nothing due, no cash figure, and a failed read

annotations.text:
THE JOB OF THIS SCREEN

It answers one question: can I commit money today, and when does that stop being true?

It is ABOUT a balance falling over time, and it drew no picture of one. The shape was left for the reader to build out of a column of figures — and the shape is the whole answer.

You settled four things and everything here follows from them.

1. THE RUNWAY IS THE SCREEN. A step line leads: today's cash, each commitment stepping it down, the low point marked, the ground below zero drawn. Everything under it is the detail — the ledger is the same walk in words, the rail says how it is worked out.

2. SAFE TO SPEND LEADS THE STRIP, not cash in hand. It is the lowest point the line reaches, it is what What to buy already budgets from, and it is the only figure here that answers "can I buy stock today". In hand is a fact you already know, and it is the number that misleads: some of it is already spent.

3. THE SCREEN CAN ACT. Three things happen here rather than being described: naming a day on an undated bill (the one act that changes the line), ringing the debtors whose money closes a gap, and saying whether a promise was kept. Today the screen has no button on it at all — it tells you to go to Creditors, to Chase debts, to Payroll, in prose.

4. THE WINDOW IS A SETTING. Thirty days is hard-coded. Every other screen in this app now carries its own window in the rail, and a shop buying on sixty-day terms reads a different horizon from one paying weekly.

Everything is drawn from index.html's own values: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, the .ow-* console components already shipping on Debtors, Creditors, Chase debts, Consignment and Pricing, and the app's own inline-SVG chart idiom. No new colour, no new weight, no new type size, no chart library.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT AS IT STANDS →

1. NO PICTURE OF THE ONE THING IT IS ABOUT. A balance falling over thirty days is a shape, and the shape is the answer — "it gets tight on the 24th" is one glance from a line and four additions from a table. The app already draws inline SVG on three other screens; this one, which needs it most, has none.

2. THE HEADLINE FIGURE IS THIRD. The strip reads in hand → promised → safe to spend → tightest day. Safe to spend is the figure the buying plan runs on and the only one that answers the question the screen exists for, and it is in the third cell at the same weight as the rest.

3. NOTHING ON THE SCREEN DOES ANYTHING. Not one button. It says "open that supplier on Creditors and tap Name a day on the bill itself" — a sentence describing a journey of four taps, for the single act that changes the forecast. It says "tap They promised… on Chase debts". It says "Open Payroll for that month". A screen that knows exactly what needs doing and can only describe it is a screen that will be read and closed.

4. A 300-CHARACTER PARAGRAPH IN THE PAGE HEAD, unmeasured, above the money. The console header is a name, one line, a hairline; the long version goes behind the "i". Seven screens already do this.

5. THREE BANDS THAT ARE THE SAME SHAPE AND MEAN DIFFERENT THINGS. Commitments, promises and undated money are all .ah-rows with the same anatomy. Only a dashed border and an italic right-hand cell separate a debtor's word from money you have promised — and the two undated rows are not events at all, they are pools, wearing a row layout that says they are.

6. THE RUNNING BALANCE IS A SENTENCE, NOT A COLUMN. "leaves 4,090,000" in a left-aligned cell of prose. The one column a person actually reads down is the one thing that is not aligned to be read down.

7. THE 30 DAYS ARE HARD-CODED. CASH_AHEAD_DAYS = 30, with no way to look further or closer.

8. THE PROMISES BAND IS FAR FROM WHAT IT QUALIFIES. It says "not counted in what is safe to spend" three hundred pixels below the figure it is talking about.

9. OFF-SYSTEM VALUES THROUGHOUT — sizes 10.5, 11.5, 12.5; radius 12 and a 4px left rail where depth in this app is hairlines; a drop shadow on the panel.

THE PROPOSAL — what changed, and why

THE LINE, AND WHY IT IS A STEP. A balance does not drift down between payments: it sits flat and drops on the day. An interpolated line would draw a shape the money never takes, and on a screen whose whole job is "when does it get tight" that is the one lie it must not tell. So every segment is horizontal and every drop is vertical, and each drop carries a dot you can hover for the payment behind it.

TWO LINES, AND WHAT SEPARATES THEM. Solid ink is what you will hold. Dashed grey is what you would hold if every promise were kept. The ghost is grey and dashed rather than green and solid, because a debtor's word is not money and must not be able to be mistaken for it at a glance — dash AND colour, so it survives being printed. Safe to spend is read off the solid line only, and the note beside the legend says so where the eye already is, rather than three hundred pixels below.

THE GROUND BELOW ZERO IS DRAWN. Not a gridline — a crimson field the line goes into. Zero is the edge of a cliff, not a tick.

THE STRIP LEADS WITH SAFE TO SPEND and says what it is measured from: "the lowest the line gets, on 24 Sep — this is what What to buy budgets from, not the 4,850,000 beside it". Naming the mistake in the tile is cheaper than the mistake.

THE LEDGER IS THE SAME WALK, IN WORDS, and the running balance is finally a column: right-aligned, tabular, in the last cell, so a person runs an eye down it and stops where it worries them. Promises sit in the same ledger in date order — dashed, and with "their word" where a balance would be, because nothing about them moves the line. Two lists became one, and the ghost line above it is the same sequence.

THE SCREEN ACTS. An undated bill carries "Name a day" on the row where you notice it is missing; opening it shows a date field and one amber line saying exactly what writing it down will do to the line and the tightest day. When the line goes under, the rail names the debtors whose money closes the gap, ranked, with the pair that covers it marked — the app's own debtsCovering derivation, which nothing has ever called from here.

THE WINDOW IS A FIELD in the rail, beside the sentence that says what it means.

MONEY WITH NO DATE IS A PAIR OF FIGURES, NOT TWO FAKE ROWS. Two pools, said as pools, with the accounting under them: what you owe in all, how much of it is already on the line, and how much is not — so a dated bill is never counted twice.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. WHETHER THE GHOST LINE SHOULD EXIST AT ALL. Drawing "if every promise is kept" makes the difference between hope and cash visible, which I think is the honest way to show it. The argument against is that the existing code's own comment warns that buying stock on a debtor's word is exactly what a forecast is meant to prevent — and a line on a chart is more persuasive than a band in a list. It is one path element and one legend row if you would rather it went.

2. THE SECOND SORT FOR WHO TO RING (see page 2's note): by what they owe, or by who actually pays.

3. WHAT "MARK A PROMISE KEPT" SHOULD DO. You asked for it and I have not drawn it, because it needs one decision I should not make: whether marking a promise kept here also POSTS the payment to the cash book, or only clears the promise and leaves the money to be recorded on Chase debts. The first is fewer taps and a real risk of a double entry; the second is safe and slightly annoying. Tell me which and it goes on the promise rows.

4. THE WINDOW'S DEFAULT stays 30. The field is there; I have not changed what it opens on.

5. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED: cashAhead and cashCommitments themselves, the safe-to-spend arithmetic, the wages-not-raised rule, and the law that only money with a real date reaches the line. All of it is right, and the redesign is about what the screen does with it.

WHEN THE LINE GOES UNDER →

The state this screen exists for, and the one the current design handles worst: today it prints a red-railed paragraph under the strip and then carries on as if nothing had happened.

THE PICTURE DOES THE WORK. The line crosses into crimson on 21 Sep and the low point is marked at 28 Sep. You do not read a figure to learn this; you see it.

THE LEDGER STARTS WHERE IT MATTERS. The four payments before the wage run leave you 450,000 and are not the problem, so they are named in one line and the list opens at the wage run. The two rows that take you under carry crimson figures and say which is which: "this is where it goes under" and "the tightest day".

WHO TO RING, RANKED, IN THE RAIL. Three debtors, what each owes, how long they have waited, and what share of the gap each closes — with the pair that covers it marked in verdigris. The accent lives here, once, as "Chase these three", and it opens Chase debts with those three at the top rather than sending anything: nothing in this app sends itself.

NAMING A DAY, OPEN. A date field on the bill, "Write it down", Cancel, and one amber line saying what it will do — 2,940,000 onto the line for 18 Sep, and the tightest day moves — and what it will not do: it pays nothing and it tells nobody.

ONE THING WORTH ARGUING WITH. The ranking for who to ring is by what they owe, oldest first where two are close. It could be by who is most likely to actually pay — the app knows who has broken promises before. I have not done that, because a ranking that quietly demotes somebody for one bad month is a ranking nobody can check. Say the word and it becomes a second sort.

THE THREE STATES A SCREEN IS ONLY DESIGNED ONCE YOU HAVE DRAWN →

NOTHING DUE IS A REAL ANSWER, AND IT IS DRAWN. A flat line at the top of the chart is the clearest possible statement that nothing is coming — better than a paragraph saying so. Three real figures stay, including the undated bills, because "nothing falls due" and "you owe nothing" are different things and a shop should never confuse them.

NO CASH FIGURE, NO LINE. What you hold is a thing somebody counts, not a thing the app can derive. If today has not been opened in the cash book there is no figure to start the line from — so the screen says that and offers the door, rather than drawing a line from a zero nobody recorded. It still names what is waiting to be drawn against it, so the state reads as incomplete rather than empty.

A PARTIAL LINE, SAID SO. If the supplier ledger fails to read, the line is missing every bill you have dated. Today the screen would simply draw the rest and look confident. So: it says what failed, when the last good read was, what that read showed, and that those are not current figures — and it WITHHOLDS safe to spend entirely. A figure missing four bills is not a cautious estimate; it is a number that would tell you to spend money you have already committed, which is the one mistake this screen exists to prevent. That is the app's own law: derived never invented, and a failure must name itself.

THE PHONE — its own design, not the table reflowed

820px is a switch, so this is drawn from scratch at 390: 44px navy bar, 26px page name, 15px body, 44px+ hit targets, no fake status bar and no fake keyboard.

THE PHONE JOB IS DIFFERENT FROM THE DESK JOB. At the desk you are planning a month. On a phone somebody is standing in front of you asking for goods on credit, or a supplier has rung to ask when. One figure answers both, so safe to spend IS the top of the screen — 34px, with the sentence that qualifies it and the shape of the month underneath.

THE CHART SURVIVES, STRIPPED. No y labels, no low-point label, no legend: the hero above already said the figures, and what the small chart adds is the shape — where it steps down, where it goes under, how long it stays there. Same geometry, a quarter of the ink.

IT IS DRAWN IN THE STATE YOU WOULD ACTUALLY PULL YOUR PHONE OUT FOR. On a healthy day this screen has nothing for you to do and no dock. Under water it has exactly one thing: ring the person whose money closes the gap. So the accent lives once, in the docked navy bar in the thumb zone — the pattern Debtors, Creditors and Follow-ups already ship — and it names who, and what they owe, so the right action is taken without reading the list.

WHAT IS NOT ON THE PHONE: naming a day. It needs a date field and a sentence about consequences, and it is a desk decision made against a list. Say the word and it becomes a sheet.

THE CHART, MADE READABLE — this pass

You said it plainly: no y axis, no x axis, no way to read it. All three were true, and they were true by an argument the code made on purpose. The old comment said "two gridlines and no more: what you hold now, and nothing left — a third would be a tick nobody reads". The opposite was the case. With only those two, every point BETWEEN them is unreadable, and the whole middle of this chart is between them.

A VALUE AXIS. Gridlines on a round step — 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten, so they land on 1,000,000 and never on 1,284,000 — with the figure at each one. Zero keeps its heavier stroke, because it is still the edge of the cliff and not a tick.

A DAY AXIS. A rule along the floor with dated ticks on it: weekly inside a month, wider as the window grows, "today" under the first and the year under the last. A step in the line can now be put on a day without counting pixels in from one end.

WHAT LEAVES EACH DAY, on the same axis. Twelve payments in thirty days piled four dots into twenty pixels, and the flat stretches between them hid how much was moving. One bar per day money goes out, sized by what goes out that day, the tightest day inked. Where two payments fall on one day the line draws one dot now, not two on top of each other.

THE TOP OF THE PLOT IS NO LONGER A ROUND NUMBER. Snapping it up to the next whole gridline put 8,000,000 above a line that never passes 6,381,779, and a quarter of the picture was empty. The domain is the data plus a little air; the gridlines are the round figures inside it.

AND THE TYPE IS THE SIZE THE RAMP SAYS. The drawing was 1000 units wide in a column that is about 800px, so every 11px label was coming out at 8.8px — small enough to be part of why none of it read. Sized to the column it comes out at 11px, and on a wider screen it scales up rather than down.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DONE, AND WOULD ASK ABOUT FIRST: a crosshair that reads the balance on any day you point at. It is the natural next thing and it is a real decision — on a phone it needs a drag, and the ledger below already answers the same question in words.
